# What Generalizes Across Design Problems {#sec-loop-patterns-across-stack}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"There is no single development, in either technology or management technique, which by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement within a decade in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity."*
>
> — Fred Brooks, *No Silver Bullet* (1987) [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Fred Brooks, Turing Award winner and author of *The
Mythical Man-Month* [@Brooks1975MythicalManMonth], warned against expecting one
technique to remove the essential difficulty of engineering. The same warning
applies when an architecture result moves to another problem. The study
structure may transfer. Its evidence does not transfer until the changed
conditions have been examined.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
When an architecture problem changes, what can transfer, what must be adapted,
what must be checked again, and what no longer supports the new decision?
:::

Architects rarely begin every design problem with an empty repository and no
prior results. A new product, workload, process, compiler, or deployment
condition often resembles work that has already been completed. Reuse can save
substantial effort. It can also preserve an obsolete assumption, stale tool
state, or conclusion that the new decision no longer supports. The useful
question is not whether the earlier work transfers as a whole. It is which
parts transfer, what changed around them, and which target checks must now run.
AI-assisted design makes that question more urgent because data, learned
components, tool wrappers, and generated artifacts can each remain usable for
different lengths of time.

Three levels of reuse keep that question precise. Principles and procedures
can transfer broadly because they organize how a new decision is studied.
Individual components transfer only when their dependencies and target checks
still support them. Conclusions do not transfer to a changed design problem
without target evidence. The durable pattern is therefore a way to reopen a
claim, not a promise that an earlier answer remains correct.

The completed study in @sec-running-the-loop supplies one concrete source
record. This chapter uses it only to illustrate a more general rule: once the
target changes, an earlier result becomes input to a new decision rather than
its conclusion.

This chapter develops a transfer test around that adaptation. It first compares
the source and target decisions, then examines individual parts of the design
system rather than moving the complete system as one unit. Later sections test
whether local gains survive the product path, whether a cheap check remains
qualified for the target, and whether hardware and software results still
apply to their current versions. The outcome is a specific action for each
part and a target check for every material change.

The recurring structure is the transfer test, not the design problem itself.
Different problems expose different permitted actions, observations,
objectives, failure classes, feedback relationships, and commitment rules. The
same procedure can organize those differences without pretending that one
taxonomy or tool sequence applies everywhere.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Compare a completed source study with a new target decision and identify the
  conditions that materially changed.
- Separate the data, represented state, methods, tools, checks, policies,
  configured system, and conclusions that might transfer, then assign each an
  appropriate reuse, refresh, rerun, adaptation, or retirement action.
- Convert every changed condition into a concrete test or an explicit untested
  boundary.
- Charge interface overhead, offload granularity, and the executable software
  path against a local result, and bound cheap checks by validated target
  coverage and the expensive work that remains.
- Keep hardware and software conclusions tied to their artifact versions,
  workloads, and conditions without treating prior conclusions as current
  results.

:::

## A New Design Problem Reopens the Claim

The source decision asked whether any of five evaluated array shapes cleared a
local score margin under one workload and simulator. The target decision asks
whether the 32 by 32 reference should determine an RTL-facing array, compiler
mapping, and memory interface for the spatial-tracking subsystem within the
Lighthouse design. This implementation-facing target is deliberately narrower
than the complete XR system. It is also not the next stage of the source claim.
It is a new claim about a more coupled artifact under a more demanding system
objective.

A *design problem* is the complete decision context in which alternatives have
meaning. It names the decision to be made and the candidate, artifact, or
system boundary to which that decision applies. It fixes the workload,
software, implementation, and system conditions; states what may and may not
change; identifies constraints and credible comparators; requires measurements
and checks; and accounts for the cost and reversibility of being wrong.

A design problem is therefore not a benchmark, candidate, method, or tool
invocation. A benchmark supplies workloads or tasks but does not decide what
the system may change. A candidate is one alternative inside the problem. A
method proposes, estimates, or selects work inside it. A tool invocation
observes a stated property under particular conditions. None carries the
decision context by itself.

A change is *material to a claim* when it can alter the candidate identity,
executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking,
constraint verdict, or mechanism on which that claim depends. Materiality is
claim-specific. A compiler update may reopen executable performance without
reopening an RTL functional property. A library or operating-corner change may
reopen timing and power without reopening a compiler-semantics result.

The source problem asked whether one of five simulated array shapes should
replace a 32 by 32 reference under a frozen local score. Its mutable boundary
was array height and width, its observation path was SCALE-Sim, and being wrong
would waste a small follow-up study. The target problem asks whether an
RTL-facing array, compiler mapping, and memory interface should be frozen for a
3\ W subsystem. Its boundary now includes software and implementation
contracts, its checks include correctness and physical behavior, and being
wrong can propagate rework across RTL, compiler, memory, and verification
teams. The same 32 by 32 artifact participates in both problems, but the
decision, conditions, required evidence, and consequence have changed.

The source record therefore carries each result forward with the boundary that
prevents it from settling the target. Reproducing that source result asks
whether the retained source computation can run again. Requalifying a
component for the target asks whether it remains supported after the problem
changes. @tbl-ch9-source-record pairs each completed source result with the
scope that survives the change in decision.

| **Source record from the completed study** | **Status carried forward** |
| --- | --- |
| Five unique shapes evaluated under a synthetic three-layer GEMM slice | Complete for that local workload and configuration; not representative of a spatial-tracking workload distribution. |
| 32 by 32 and 16 by 64 tie on the frozen local score | No-change result for the five evaluated shapes; not an implementation ranking. |
| Model and weak fixed heuristic tie at equal simulator-call budgets | No study-local AI advantage; no result about another proposer or repeated runs. |
| Directional mechanism prediction fails its contrast | Failed recorded explanation; no replacement mechanism established. |
| SCALE-Sim reports cycles, utilization, and modeled word traffic | Cycle-accurate simulator outputs; no measured energy, RTL, timing, congestion, or thermal result. |
| Retain 32 by 32 and stop the local search | Technical recommendation remains pending and cannot settle the target decision. |

: **The source record carries both reusable results and their limits.** The
evaluated shapes, local comparison, failed explanation, simulator outputs, and
pending recommendation remain tied to the source workload, configuration,
observability, and decision boundary. {#tbl-ch9-source-record tbl-colwidths="[47,43]"}

The first three rows preserve the evaluated shapes, local score, and proposer
comparison while limiting each conclusion to the completed study. The last
three retain the failed explanation, the simulator's observability boundary,
and the pending recommendation. The record supports reuse of artifacts and
provenance, not an implementation ranking.

The target question is deliberately specific.

> Should the 32 by 32 reference, together with its compiler-visible tiling and
> memory-interface contract, be frozen for RTL implementation in the
> Lighthouse subsystem?

The target keeps the Lighthouse conditions fixed, including the 64-bit RISC-V
hardware-software basis and the 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process. The new
study must pin the selected process design kit, standard-cell and memory
libraries, and process, voltage, and temperature conditions before it can make
an implementation claim.

The answer cannot be read directly from the source record. A frozen interface
affects the compiler, SRAM organization, interconnect traffic, host behavior,
power, and future software. A simulated shape can be discarded cheaply. An
RTL and software contract can trigger downstream rework even before tapeout.
The obligations add rather than replace one another. Every source result keeps
its local meaning, while each source check must be reassessed before it is used
for the target. Every changed condition adds another question the target study
must answer.

The source and target therefore share artifacts without sharing a complete
decision. The simulator outputs, workload records, candidate definitions, and
tool configuration can be inspected separately from the represented project
state, proposing and checking methods, tool interfaces, environment, and
conclusions. This component view matters because two neighboring parts can
transfer differently. A simulator wrapper may remain correct while its
calibration expires, or a predictor may retain useful structure while the
decision it previously supported no longer applies.

## Changed Conditions Create Test Obligations

The adaptation becomes concrete when each changed condition produces a test
obligation rather than a vague demand for more rigor
(@tbl-ch9-source-target).

| **Condition** | **Completed source study** | **Implementation-facing target** | **Obligation created by the change** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Result cost and delay | Seconds-scale cycle-accurate simulation and replay in the completed run | Compiler experiments, RTL, synthesis, floorplanning, and routed checks | Use the simulator for screening; budget slower checks and the review needed to interpret them. |
| Reversibility | A simulated shape can be discarded | An array and interface freeze creates downstream software and hardware rework | Keep 32 by 32 provisional and preserve a fallback until target checks settle. |
| Coupling and interface span | Array dimensions varied while mapping and interfaces stayed fixed | Compiler mapping, SRAM, interconnect, host, and accelerator contracts interact | Measure the executable software path and end-to-end offload cost. |
| Observability and check independence | Cycles, utilization, and modeled word traffic from one simulator | Correctness, latency, bandwidth, area, timing, congestion, power, thermal behavior, reliability, and security properties required by the target | Add memory-system, RTL, implementation, thermal, fault, and security checks where the target consequence requires them; derive checks separately where practical and disclose shared assumptions. |
| Consequence | A local no-change recommendation | A 3\ W subsystem commitment affecting later implementation | Replace the local score with target criteria and state what remains untested. |
| Workload | Synthetic three-layer XR-like GEMM slice | Trace-backed spatial-tracking distribution, including tails and drift | Rebuild workload coverage; do not treat the source slice as representative. |
| Software turnover | One frozen mapping and tool configuration | Compiler and runtime versions will continue to change | Version hardware and software together and rerun affected claims after material changes. |
| Review capacity and ownership | The source team has the expertise, tool access, review time, and decision rights needed to challenge the study. | The target organization may assign different people, access, budgets, or authority. | Confirm that the target team can operate and challenge the transferred system, then reassign review and decision rights where needed. |

: **Changed conditions accumulate test obligations.** The target study keeps
the source record but cannot inherit the source conclusion. {#tbl-ch9-source-target tbl-colwidths="[15,23,25,37]"}

The first three
rows move from a cheap, reversible, isolated simulation to slower checks and
a coupled executable path. The next two add observations and decision
consequences that the local score did not carry. The final three reopen workload
coverage, hardware-software versioning, and the capacity to operate and
challenge the design process. These are the material conditions for this
adaptation, not an exhaustive taxonomy of design problems. One
relation explains why they matter. The
expected loss from accepting a transferred result is approximately the
probability that the acceptance is false multiplied by the loss conditional on
that false acceptance. That loss includes reversal and rework cost plus any
consequence that cannot be reversed. Workload mismatch, limited observability,
and unsupported proxies raise the first factor. Interface coupling, downstream
commitment, and system consequence raise the second. Some changes raise both.
The complete decision also prices false rejection, missed benefit, and the
cost of requalification. A policy that prevents every false acceptance by
rejecting every transfer is not useful.

Artifacts need not change for a ranking to change. A revised objective,
normalization, feasibility constraint, or dominance rule can reorder the same
candidates. Such a change reopens the decision even when the workload, tool
outputs, and candidate files remain identical.

Security and reliability do not enter every study through a universal
checklist. They enter when the target's assets, threat model, failure model, or
consequence of failure makes them part of the architecture decision.

This comparison supplies a general procedure. Name the source and target
decisions, compare the material conditions, and retain every obligation created
by a material difference. A category such as software, RTL, or physical design
does not settle the comparison on its own. The same artifact can require
different evidence when its workload, interface, or consequence changes.

The source workload is useful because its dimensions are explicit, not because
it represents a real spatial-tracking pipeline. The target therefore needs a
trace-backed workload distribution, coverage of common and tail shapes, and a
versioned account of the compiler and runtime that produce those shapes. The
MICA workload-characterization method established why benchmark suites must
separate inherent workload properties from artifacts of one machine
[@HosteEeckhout2007MICA]. The same discipline applies here. A target claim
must say which workload properties are covered and which remain outside the
study.

The mapping semantics must also be explicit. The completed source study
disclosed that the surviving prompt copy had not pinned how GEMM dimensions
map to array dimensions, and the exact recorded prompt could not be verified.
The new study must bind those dimensions in both the compiler path and
simulator configuration before it compares shapes. AutoTVM and Ansor show how measured
compiler searches join schedules, cost models, and executable targets
[@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. Their relevance here is not that
one of those systems should be selected. It is that the target decision
depends on the schedule and hardware together.

The source study never entered RTL or physical design. The target would, so
its observability and reversal costs change. Compiler execution and
architecture simulation remain useful early checks, but they cannot observe
whether an RTL block is synthesizable, whether its interface is correct, or
whether the routed design meets timing, power, and thermal constraints.

The target study therefore needs an implementation path whose checks match the
claims at risk. Functional simulation exercises selected cases. Independently
derived formal properties can prove stated behavior within their assumptions,
while equivalence checks can establish a specified relation between
representations. Lint and synthesis expose structural and legality failures.
Physical implementation checks setup and hold timing across relevant corners,
congestion, design rules, signal integrity, and power-delivery limits. When the
target decision carries reliability or security consequences, the path must
also state the relevant fault and threat models, then exercise the protection,
recovery, isolation, and information-flow properties derived from them.

This is neither a universal sequence nor a monotonic rise in confidence.
Simulation, proof, equivalence, synthesis, floorplanning, routing, extraction,
and signoff operate on different representations and observe different failure
classes. A later return can invalidate earlier RTL, constraints, mappings, or
interfaces and force the study to re-enter an earlier part of the path. None
alone establishes implementation readiness.

Wire effects make the escalation substantive. Synthesis and physical
synthesis can include wire estimates, but those estimates do not replace
extracted routed behavior. Global-wire delay grows relative to gate delay under
scaling, and repeater-based mitigation carries area and power costs
[@HoMaiHorowitz2001FutureOfWires]. The target must therefore test whether the
source ordering survives placement, routing, and the memory path rather than
assume every earlier proxy is optimistic in the same direction.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Timing closure does not settle the thermal question"}
A Lighthouse datapath could meet the conventional timing corners used by one
flow and still fail a coupled power-density or electrothermal check because
the headset has little cooling capacity. A timing result supports only the
corners and thermal assumptions it actually modeled. The target study must add
the missing analysis instead of reading it into a clean timing report.
:::

Lower reversibility also creates a design obligation. A bypass, feature
disable, voltage or frequency guardband, or spare-cell allowance can reduce
specific failure costs, but no one mechanism repairs every datapath,
interface, timing, or routing defect. The target must identify the credible
failure classes first and then test the containment mechanism intended for
each one.

Intel's 2011 recall announcement documents a 6-series chipset defect, the
shipment stop, the planned silicon correction, and an estimated \$700 million
repair and replacement cost [@Intel2011CougarPoint].

::: {.callout-war-story title="A correction has to reach the failure"}
**The claim.** Intel stated that consumers could continue using affected
systems while manufacturers arranged a permanent solution.

**The gap.** A silicon defect could cause some ports to degrade. Intel stopped
shipments and prepared corrected silicon rather than treating the problem as a
software-only failure.

**The lesson.** The permanent correction used revised silicon and repair or
replacement. A containment or correction mechanism is useful only when it can
reach the component and failure mode that threaten the target system.
:::

Independent checking should reduce shared assumptions rather than merely
repeat the generation path. The target should derive functional properties and
reference behavior separately from the generated RTL where possible, document
model and prompt lineage, and measure correlated failures when complete
independence is unavailable. A separate specification reading, synthesis
flow, formal property set, or implementation check can expose a different
failure class without being treated as ground truth.

Learned synthesis studies and a vendor-reported physical-design search
demonstrate bounded proposal and search roles within these stages
[@RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL; @Synopsys2023DSOai]. Each proposal must still reach the target check that can
observe its relevant failure class. The study record must retain tool versions,
failed candidates, check results, and untested boundaries.

## What Part of the Design System Transfers?

A source-to-target comparison becomes actionable only when it names the unit
being transferred. Data, project state, methods, tools, checks, and conclusions
do not share one lifetime. Treating them as a single package forces an
unhelpful choice between copying everything and starting over.
@tbl-ch9-transfer-map separates the units that commonly appear in an
AI-assisted architecture study. For each unit, it asks what dependency changed,
which action remains valid, and what target check is needed before the unit can
support new work.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data, records, and current knowledge** | Workload, design space, objectives, provenance, collection conditions, specifications, manuals, libraries, or project documents differ. | Reuse the historical record; refresh target data and sources; retire stale sources; narrow unsupported coverage. | Check trace and artifact provenance, source identity and version, target coverage and exclusions, source-to-target overlap, and whether retrieved material supports the target fact. |
| **Representation and project state** | Constraints, interfaces, artifact versions, or cross-layer relationships differ. | Refresh live state; adapt the representation; replace a representation that hides a required relationship. | Check schema and constraint completeness, version consistency, and integration with neighboring state. |
| **Learned component** | Training support, inputs, outputs, objectives, constraints, project facts, or data-generating conditions changed. | Requalify the unchanged component; rerun a generator or optimizer; recalibrate a numerical mapping; adapt, retrain, replace, or retire the component when needed. | Test every role it fills on held-out target tasks, including accuracy or calibration, candidate legality, objective quality, stale knowledge, failure classes, and performance against the declared comparator. |
| **Conventional method** | Analytical assumptions, solver formulation, design space, or objective changed. | Reuse, adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the method. | Check its assumptions on the target and compare its target result with the same decision rule used for other methods. |
| **Tool interface and environment component** | Command syntax, parameter meaning, output schema, status codes, tool or library version, constraint and configuration files, random seed, license, runtime, machine resource, reset behavior, or isolation changed. | Refresh configuration; adapt, replace, or retire the component; rerun affected work. | Check target-version execution, interface parsing and failure classification, constraints and stochastic state, reset and isolation behavior, resource accounting, and integration with connected tools. |
| **Empirical screening check** | Target coverage, observed conditions, error tolerance, or relationship to the target reference changed. | Requalify before reuse; recalibrate only when a numerical mapping or threshold changes; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Measure target support and class-specific errors against a separate reference capable of observing the property at risk. |
| **Formal, equivalence, deterministic, or rule-based check** | The target specification, assumptions, properties, representation relation, rules, or tool version changed. | Review the specification mapping; requalify the target setup; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Check property and assumption coverage, the relation being established, target tool integration, and known positive, negative, and inconclusive cases. |
| **Routing or escalation policy** | Check cost, consequence, qualified coverage, or available review capacity changed. | Adapt, replace, narrow, or retire the policy. | Exercise routing thresholds, uncertain cases, failure injection, escalation, and resource limits on the target. |
| **Complete configured technical system** | Any neighboring component or interface changed, even when this configuration did not. | Rerun target integration; adapt, replace, narrow, or reject the configuration when required. | Repeat the end-to-end target task with pinned versions, total product-path costs, failures, and a credible alternative. |
| **Architecture and AI-contribution conclusions** | The target decision, comparator, budget, or measured path differs from the source. | Narrow the conclusion to its supported source scope or reject its transfer. | Repeat the architecture comparison and the matched AI-contribution comparison under target conditions. |

: **Transfer decisions are component-specific.** A unit moves only with an
action suited to the dependency that changed and a target check capable of
observing the resulting risk. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-map tbl-colwidths="[20,27,25,28]"}

The information, methods, executable environment, checks, and configured
system can receive different dispositions. The last row is different because a
conclusion is not a component that can be updated mechanically. It must be
narrowed to the conditions already tested or rejected for the new decision.

Only learned components can be retrained. Data can be refreshed, a
representation can be adapted, a tool interface can be replaced, and a check
can be recalibrated, but none of those actions is retraining unless the unit
itself learns from data. A broadly trained architecture model can contribute
general knowledge about candidate structures or propose candidates, while a
specialized model can predict, generate, optimize, or check. One learned
component can fill several roles and inherits
the target obligations of every role it fills. No learned prior carries live
project state, current tool checks, or architecture conclusions inside itself.
Those remain explicit target artifacts.

The check rows do not imply equal claim strength. A formal proof establishes
only the stated properties under its assumptions. An equivalence check
establishes a specified relation between representations. A deterministic
analysis reports the quantities it implements, while a rule-based heuristic
supplies no proof merely because it is repeatable. Passing target-version
regressions can qualify tool integration, but it does not enlarge formal
property coverage or make a heuristic sound.

An unchanged component still needs an integration check after a neighbor
changes. A wrapper that parses the same simulator correctly may receive new
parameters from a revised representation. A verifier with unchanged code may
observe artifacts produced by a new generator. Component identity alone does
not establish compatibility with the new configured system.

Qualification also does not compose automatically. Several components can pass
their individual target checks and still fail together because they share
training data, representations, tool assumptions, or blind spots. The
configured system therefore needs an end-to-end target check, and its
confidence argument must account for correlated failures rather than treating
component results as independent.

Technical reuse can also fail operationally. A target team may lack the tool
access, operating knowledge, review capacity, or authority needed to challenge
a transferred component when it fails. The transfer plan must expose those
conditions and stop when they are absent; the later ownership discussion
conditions. The transfer cannot support operation or approval until missing
access, expertise, capacity, or authority is supplied. The later ownership
discussion determines who holds the corresponding decisions.

## Local Gains Must Survive End-to-End Product Costs

The source study varied the compute array while holding the simulator
dataflow, configuration, and interface parameters fixed. It did not execute a
compiler or complete software path. The target cannot leave that path
implicit. A specialization result is useful only if a stable workload reaches
the block through executable software and each offload performs enough work to
repay the interface cost. These are target obligations created by coupling,
workload turnover, and the 3\ W system constraint.

Here, end-to-end product cost means the cost paid along the implemented
product path. It includes startup latency, data movement, compiler and runtime
effects, interface overhead, operating power, and the software needed to keep
the path usable. It is distinct from the design-workflow cost of model calls,
tool runs, human review, and failed proposals. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect
later compares those workflow costs. This section asks whether the proposed
architecture improvement survives once the product itself executes.

A specialization case should answer six questions together
(@fig-domain-specificity-shapes). How stable is the kernel family? Which data
types and precision changes must the datapath tolerate? How predictable is
memory behavior? How durable is the program interface? Which deployment and
quality-of-service targets apply? How much workload drift and verification
cost can the design absorb? A weak answer raises cost or requires
programmability and fallback. It does not prove that specialization is
impossible.

![**Six questions test whether a specialization case is durable.** Kernel stability, data and precision, memory behavior, program interface, deployment targets, and drift and verification each create an obligation. Flexibility can mitigate a weak condition, but its cost belongs in the target comparison.](images/F9a-domain-specificity-shapes){#fig-domain-specificity-shapes width="100%" fig-alt="Central question about what is stable enough to specialize, surrounded by kernel family, data and precision, memory behavior, program interface, deployment and quality-of-service, and drift and verification."}

Kernel family, data and precision, and memory behavior determine whether the
computation has a stable shape. Program interface, deployment targets, and
drift and verification determine whether that shape remains usable after it
leaves the local kernel. The central claim depends on both groups. A weak
condition does not rule out specialization, but its flexibility, fallback, and
verification costs belong in the product-path comparison.

An author-derived Amdahl-style expression makes the end-to-end obligation
explicit [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. Normalize all terms to the
baseline execution time and assume that the listed compute, interface, and
software costs add without overlap:
$$
S_{\mathrm{system}} \le
\frac{1}{(1-\phi) + \phi/s + \epsilon_{\mathrm{interface}} + \epsilon_{\mathrm{software}}}.
$$
Here, $\phi$ is the improvable fraction of baseline time, $s$ is local
speedup, and the $\epsilon$ terms are interface and software overheads under
that normalization. The inequality allows omitted nonnegative costs. It becomes
an equality only when the expression includes every additive cost and the
no-overlap assumption holds. A useful decomposition is
$\epsilon_{\mathrm{interface}} = (N L_{\mathrm{startup}} +
\text{Data Volume}/\text{Bandwidth})/T_{\mathrm{baseline}}$. Too many
invocations or too much data movement can erase the local compute gain. For
the Lighthouse target, the implementation-readiness study must measure whether
trace-backed spatial-tracking work reaches the array at a granularity and
locality compatible with the 3\ W budget.

A simplified LogCA-style calculation resolves the same tax by offload
granularity [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. Let normalized host time be
$T_{\mathrm{host}} = g$ for work amount $g$. Let accelerator time be
$T_{\mathrm{acc}} = o + g/A + bg$, where $o$ is fixed startup time, $A$ is
local compute acceleration, and $b$ is transfer time per work unit. The
plotted speedup is therefore

$$
S(g) = \frac{g}{o + g/A + bg}.
$$

The three parameter sets in @fig-logca-breakeven are illustrative. They show
how startup and transfer terms change break-even behavior, not measured
properties of three attachment classes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-logca-breakeven
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Offload conditions determine the break-even granularity.** In this illustrative LogCA-style model [@AltafWood2017LogCA], end-to-end speedup appears only after each offload performs enough work to amortize startup and transfer cost.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Line plot showing offload speedup curves that rise only after enough work is amortized to overcome interface latency and overhead."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, add_note_box, apply_style

apply_style()

A = 100.0
g = [10 ** (6 * i / 399) for i in range(400)]

curves = [
    {"label": "tightly coupled accelerator", "ovh": 2.0, "bw_penalty": 0.0, "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"label": "shared-memory SoC block", "ovh": 40.0, "bw_penalty": 0.005, "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"label": "off-chip / discrete module", "ovh": 1500.0, "bw_penalty": 0.05, "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

def speedup(gran, ovh, bw_penalty):
    return gran / (ovh + gran / A + gran * bw_penalty)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.25, 3.12))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.86, top=0.82, bottom=0.28)

ax.axhline(A, color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.text(1.35, A * 1.08, "peak acceleration A", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=6.2, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.text(7.5e5, 1.10, "break-even", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"])

ax.axhspan(0.25, 1.0, color=COLORS["red"], alpha=0.08, zorder=0)
ax.text(1.5, 0.38, "offload loses", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["red"], fontstyle="italic")

for c in curves:
    s = [speedup(x, c["ovh"], c["bw_penalty"]) for x in g]
    ax.plot(g, s, color=c["color"], linewidth=1.9, zorder=3, label=c["label"])
    denom = 1.0 - 1.0 / A - c["bw_penalty"]
    g1 = c["ovh"] / denom if denom > 0 else 1e9
    if g1 < 1e6:
        ax.scatter([g1], [1.0], marker="o", s=22, facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=c["color"], linewidth=1.3, zorder=4, clip_on=False)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1, 1e6)
ax.set_ylim(0.25, 150)
ax.set_xlabel("operation granularity  (work amortized per offload)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("end-to-end speedup", fontsize=7)
ax.set_yticks([0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100])
ax.set_yticklabels([r"0.3$\times$", r"1$\times$", r"3$\times$", r"10$\times$", r"30$\times$", r"100$\times$"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2, labelsize=6.4)
ax.grid(axis="both", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

legend = fig.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=6.0, frameon=False,
                    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), handlelength=1.0, columnspacing=1.4)
for text in legend.get_texts():
    text.set_color(COLORS["ink"])

add_note_box(
    fig,
    "Illustrative parameter sets: larger startup and transfer terms require more work per offload before acceleration breaks even.",
    xywh=(0.10, 0.03, 0.80, 0.11),
    fontsize=5.5,
)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The three curves apply progressively larger illustrative startup and transfer
terms to the same local compute acceleration. The first breaks even after
little work per offload, the second needs more, and the third needs far more.
The transfer term also lowers the ceiling. In the third parameter set, the
curve saturates at roughly 17x against the 100x local compute acceleration.
The causal variables are the modeled interface terms rather than physical
distance alone. A local result can vanish once the target charges the real
per-invocation path.

Offload granularity and arithmetic intensity bound different parts of this
result. Increasing the work per offload amortizes the fixed startup term in the
LogCA-style model. Arithmetic intensity determines the separate Roofline
bandwidth ceiling, which bounds attainable performance by the lesser of peak
compute and arithmetic intensity times memory bandwidth
[@Williams2009Roofline]. A generated kernel below the machine's balance
point,[^fn-machine-balance-c09] moving roughly a byte for every operation on a
bandwidth-limited link, remains bandwidth-bound after startup has been
amortized. It may still provide an end-to-end speedup, but it cannot reach the
local compute ceiling. The target must therefore test both the per-invocation
latency cost and the data-movement bound before promoting the specialization.

[^fn-machine-balance-c09]: **Machine balance point**: The arithmetic intensity, measured in operations performed per byte of memory traffic, at which a machine's peak compute rate and its peak memory bandwidth are exactly matched. A kernel below that ratio stays bandwidth-bound no matter how fast the compute units run, and a kernel above it becomes compute-bound, which is the ridge where the Roofline curve bends from one regime into the other.

The software path connects domain intent to hardware. Programming models,
compiler intermediate representations (IRs), libraries, runtimes, and
generated code form the core construction path shown in
@fig-codegen-narrow-waist.

![**A software path to specialized hardware.** Domain-specific architectural claims require executable software paths and evidence about correctness, performance, portability, and maintenance.](images/F9b-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="92%" fig-alt="Narrow-waist diagram showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting specialized hardware to evidence checks."}

Domain intent and the workload distribution meet the architecture mechanisms
and hardware constraints before they reach the code-generation waist. The
programming model, compiler
representations, libraries, runtime, and generated code then carry the
specialization into an executable path. Tools can measure correctness and
performance on a declared target. Portability requires repeated target
configurations, while maintainability requires evidence from change, repair,
rebuild, and human review.

The figure is deliberately a narrow waist, not a complete system-software
inventory. A target may also depend on operating-system services, device
drivers, firmware, memory management, synchronization, and deployment
configuration. A local kernel result cannot bypass the parts of that path that
carry its claim. The target study must retain the hardware and lowering path,
then record the kernel, schedule, compiler, runtime, driver and firmware
versions where applicable, interface, and hardware version that produced each
result.

That hardware-interface boundary matters because a candidate can look strong
in isolation and still collapse once the compiler, data movement, and
end-to-end path are accounted for. Consider a generated block that posts a
large kernel speedup while the compiler cannot keep it busy, data movement
dominates, and only hand-written code reaches the headline result. The target
study must include the interface and software path, then require a
compiler-generated end-to-end measurement before promoting the candidate.
That executable must also preserve the intended numerics, memory-ordering
rules, application binary interface, device-interface semantics, and workload
meaning. A fast lowering that changes the computation is not a transferred
speedup.

## Cheap Checks Help Only Within Validated Coverage

SCALE-Sim remains a valid measurement and replay path for the source
configurations it already evaluated. Using it to screen new target workloads or
candidates requires a new target qualification. This section does not ask
whether a cheap check is useful in general. It asks whether this particular
check can settle a declared share of target cases within stated error limits.
The simulator cannot establish physical
energy, timing, congestion, or end-to-end software cost. A sampled set of
target candidates therefore needs a higher-fidelity reference path that can
reveal where the cheap ordering stops holding. ArchGym and Apollo demonstrate
why architecture searches use common interfaces and transferred evaluations
to reduce expensive simulation
[@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym; @yazdanbakhsh2021apollo]. Transfer saves work only
after the target checks show which source relationships still hold.

Here, *higher fidelity* is property-specific rather than a global rank. A
simulator, formal proof, equivalence check, extracted timing run, thermal
analysis, and silicon measurement observe different quantities under different
assumptions. They can be complementary or incomparable. The target reference
must be capable of observing the property and failure class that qualify the
cheap check.

The target plan sends some candidates through cheap screening and others
through expensive reference checks. A generator that increases proposal
volume without increasing qualified review capacity grows a queue rather than
useful progress. Long-running functional-verification surveys report that
verification already consumes a large share of ASIC project effort
[@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Any claimed productivity gain must
therefore include the checks and review induced by the additional candidates.

An Amdahl-like expected service-work model describes a fixed stream of
comparable candidates [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor;
@AltafWood2017LogCA]. Let $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$ be the mean service cost when every
item goes to a high-fidelity reference, and let $c_{\mathrm{cheap}} <
c_{\mathrm{hi}}$ be the mean cost of a cheaper check. Let $f$ be the fraction
of items from a declared target distribution routed to a region where the
cheaper check settles the case within predeclared class-specific false-accept
and false-reject limits.
Let $a$ be the fraction that incurs the cheap check. The service-work speedup
is

$$
S_{\mathrm{review}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + a \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon} \le \frac{1}{(1-f) + f \cdot (c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}}) + \epsilon}.
$$

The dimensionless overhead $\epsilon \ge 0$ is mean per-item routing, audit,
and rework cost normalized by $c_{\mathrm{hi}}$. Queueing delay is excluded
because it is a latency effect rather than service work.

The inequality holds because $f \le a$. A candidate cannot be settled by a
check that never ran on it, so substituting $f$ for $a$ can only shrink the
denominator. The bound is attained only when every paid cheap check settles
the case within the declared error limits and no cheap-check work is spent on
items that later escalate. Incorrectly accepted items cannot disappear from
the accounting. They must count as failures against those error limits or the
comparison with the all-reference baseline is invalid.

The bound's best case assumes an ideal router that knows which items the cheap
check will settle. A practical system must infer support or abstain before it
knows the reference result. That routing gate is another predictor. It needs
target qualification, and false routing must enter both the class-specific
error limits and the service-work calculation.

Validated coverage is therefore not an intrinsic property of the cheap check.
It depends on the target distribution, sampling plan, routing policy, and
abstention rule. Estimating it only on cases the router accepts creates
selection bias. Qualification needs representative samples from accepted,
escalated, and abstained regions, or probability weighting by each region's
target mass, so the reported $f$ describes the target stream rather than the
router's easiest cases.

As $c_{\mathrm{cheap}}/c_{\mathrm{hi}} \to 0$ and $\epsilon = 0$, the
free-check ceiling approaches $1/(1-f)$. No reduction in unit check cost can
lift that ceiling without increasing validated coverage. The model bounds
expected service work. It becomes a throughput bound only when the modeled
work consumes the bottleneck resource under stated capacity and concurrency
assumptions.

@fig-rejection-bound-ceiling makes this limit visible. At any fixed validated
coverage \(f\), lower check cost moves the colored curves toward the dashed
ceiling, but only broader validated coverage moves the ceiling itself.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rejection-bound-ceiling
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Validated coverage sets the upper bound.** In this zero-overhead service-work model, a check that settles more target cases within declared error limits raises the ceiling.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of review service-cost speedup against validated coverage f on the x-axis. A dashed ceiling curve traces one over one minus f, and three colored cost-ratio curves for 0.01, 0.1, and 0.3 sit below it; an annotated point marks f equals 0.6 capping the speedup at about 2.5x."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, add_note_box, apply_style

apply_style()

f_grid = [0.95 * i / 399 for i in range(400)]
ratios = [
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.01", "r": 0.01, "color": COLORS["orange"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.1", "r": 0.1, "color": COLORS["green"]},
    {"label": "cost ratio 0.3", "r": 0.3, "color": COLORS["red"]},
]

def s_review(cov, r, a):
    return 1.0 / ((1.0 - cov) + a * r)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.25, 3.12))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.86, top=0.82, bottom=0.28)

ceiling = [1.0 / (1.0 - x) for x in f_grid]
ax.fill_between(f_grid, ceiling, 30, color=COLORS["grid"], alpha=0.35, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.04, 9.0, "unreachable without more validated coverage", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"], fontstyle="italic")
ax.plot(f_grid, ceiling, color=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)

ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.text(0.93, 1.04, "no speedup", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["muted"])

for c in ratios:
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], x) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.9, zorder=3, label=c["label"])
    ax.plot(f_grid, [s_review(x, c["r"], 1.0) for x in f_grid], color=c["color"], linewidth=1.2, linestyle=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=3)

ax.scatter([0.6], [2.5], marker="o", s=22, facecolor=COLORS["note_fill"], edgecolor=COLORS["ink"], linewidth=1.3, zorder=4)
ax.text(0.58, 2.95, "f = 0.6 caps the speedup at 2.5x", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.0, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0, 0.95)
ax.set_ylim(0.7, 30)
ax.set_xlabel("validated coverage f  (share of cases settled without escalation)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("review service-work speedup", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8])
ax.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20])
ax.set_yticklabels(["1x", "2x", "5x", "10x", "20x"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2, labelsize=6.4)
ax.grid(axis="both", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

legend = ax.legend(
    loc="lower left",
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.02),
    fontsize=6.0,
    frameon=True,
    facecolor="white",
    edgecolor="white",
    framealpha=0.92,
    handlelength=1.6,
    borderpad=0.15,
    labelspacing=0.3,
    ncol=1,
)
for text in legend.get_texts():
    text.set_color(COLORS["ink"])

add_note_box(
    fig,
    "Solid curves show an ideal router that pays for the cheap check only where it settles the case (a = f); dashed color curves screen every candidate (a = 1). The black dashed line is the free-check ceiling 1/(1-f).",
    xywh=(0.10, 0.03, 0.80, 0.11),
    fontsize=5.5,
)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The zero-overhead plot makes the bound visible
(@fig-rejection-bound-ceiling). The x-axis is validated coverage, the fraction
of target cases the cheaper check settles within declared error limits without
escalation, and the y-axis is expected service-work speedup. The dashed black
line is the free-check ceiling, $1/(1-f)$. Each color fixes a different ratio
between cheap-check and reference cost. The solid curve routes the cheap check
only where it settles the case, while the matching dashed curve screens every
candidate and pays for checks that later escalate. Every case outside
validated coverage still pays the high-fidelity cost. At $f = 0.6$, a free
check cannot exceed 2.5x in this model. A reported review-speedup claim
therefore needs coverage, class-specific error bounds, the sampling and
confidence calculation behind them, and the cost ratio. A consequential
decision should use a conservative lower confidence bound on supported coverage
rather than the point estimate of $f$.

Service work does not by itself predict iteration time. Under a simple M/M/1
model, normalized queue wait is $\rho/(1-\rho)$
[@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems], so the target study also needs review-capacity
headroom or admission control. The complete workflow evaluation in
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect owns the stronger queueing and latency claim.

## Hardware and Software Results Remain Version-Bound

The target widens the causal chain from one array parameter to the compiler,
runtime, memory system, and host. Hardware and software snapshots must
therefore be versioned together, and local objectives must be checked against
the Lighthouse system objective.

A single-layer optimization can be locally correct and still make the complete
system worse. Modern cross-layer work includes algorithmic tiling around the
memory hierarchy [@DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention] and pairing narrow numerical
formats with hardware-efficiency and accuracy objectives
[@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. In the Lighthouse system, compute capability
and camera-interface bandwidth must both support the frame target. Holding
either hardware or software fixed restricts the available choices and can hide
tradeoffs that joint design would expose. A throughput improvement that
violates latency or bandwidth constraints remains unacceptable.

Software feedback supports the target claim only when the run record ties each
code path to the hardware snapshot it targeted. In many flows, software tuning
returns sooner than implementation checks. The two paths must stay
joined by one study record so the fast path cannot replace the slower checks
(@fig-hardware-software-coevolution).

![**Recording hardware and software state.** Hardware target state and software path state evolve together through a shared study record, ensuring fast software tuning does not replace slower hardware checks.](images/F9c-hardware-software-coevolution){#fig-hardware-software-coevolution width="100%" fig-alt="Two-lane diagram of hardware target state and software path state evolving together through a shared study record and target review."}

The hardware target exposes legal knobs to the software interface, while
generated kernels and schedules can reveal pressure to revise the hardware
snapshot. The arrow
labeled "changes target" represents a proposed revision. The shared study
record and decision-holder review determine whether that revision becomes new
target state. Both paths return through review, so a fast software result can
reopen the hardware question without silently overwriting it.

The figure does not prescribe a synchronized universal loop. Hardware and
software can advance at different cadences. Each result remains bound to an
immutable hardware-software version pair, and review joins only claims whose
dependencies intersect rather than serializing every change through one fixed
cycle.

In this figure, software state includes the compiler, runtime, interface, and
generated artifacts. A target whose execution also depends on drivers,
firmware, operating-system services, or device control must version those
elements in the same lane.

Design-time results, deployment telemetry, and later software enablement are
scoped to the artifact versions and conditions they observe, and they support
different claims. A simulator result belongs to the candidate and conditions it
evaluated. Field telemetry belongs to the shipped hardware-software version and
deployed workload. A later compiler or firmware result belongs to the revised
software path and the hardware version it targets. The study record keeps these
returns related but separately scoped so a newer signal does not silently
overwrite an older result.

A new workload, compiler, runtime, mapping, interface, firmware, model,
constraint set, or tool version does not reopen every result automatically. It
reopens the claims whose inputs, path, observation, or interpretation it can
change.

A material change to the action space, objective, specification, interface
semantics, or measurement meaning is not merely a statistical distribution
shift. It changes the task or the decision itself; reweighting data or
retraining a model cannot repair that mismatch. Machine learning gives useful
names to three responses when the task definition remains coherent. Distribution
shift describes a change in the data-generating conditions between source and target
[@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. Robustness asks whether a component
remains acceptable without modification under the declared target variation.
Adaptation changes a component, while
target evaluation determines whether that change restored support. Keeping the
three ideas separate prevents every changed condition from becoming an
automatic retraining request. A tool, process, specification, representation,
or interface change can still invalidate a learned mapping even when observed
feature distributions appear stable.

The response should match the changed unit. Refresh data, documents, or live
project state when their contents changed. *Requalify* an unchanged component
to test whether its stated support still holds on the target. *Recalibrate* only
when fitting a numerical mapping, confidence estimate, score-to-risk
relationship, or threshold. Recalibration cannot recover a missing feature or
repair invalid semantics. Adapt a representation, interface, method
configuration, or policy when its structure still fits but its target details
do not. Retrain only a learned component, and only when target data and a
held-out check justify doing so. Replace or retire a model, method, tool, or
check that no longer has adequate support.

Only dependent claims reopen. For the changed target, those claims expire
until the appropriate refresh, rerun, requalification, recalibration,
adaptation, retraining, replacement, or retirement is complete and the target
check passes. Unaffected
claims remain scoped to their original versions and conditions, although a
changed neighbor still requires an integration check. The old result remains
historical evidence. It is not deleted or silently relabeled as current. The
record should name the change that triggered review, the dependent claims that
reopened, and the claims judged unaffected so version churn does not force
indiscriminate repetition.

Rollback must restore the configured dependency set, not only model weights.
If a schema, representation, compiler, runtime, interface, tool, library, or
hardware target changed, returning to an earlier learned component without its
compatible configuration does not restore the earlier system.

Attributed field observations can motivate a new calibration study for a
later hardware generation. They do not update a surrogate or design rule
automatically. The calibration study must bind each observation to the shipped
hardware, software, workload cohort, and measurement conditions, keep
calibration cases separate from held-out checks, and test whether the deployed
cohort covers the next target. The deployed workload is a selected sample of
what the earlier system happened to serve. When a learned predictor is reused,
a changed workload or operating-condition distribution is an architecture
instance of distribution shift. Fitting it without those checks can narrow the
next design around yesterday's traffic.

NVIDIA reported workload-specific single-node training improvements on the
same H100 hardware between the MLPerf Training v2.1 preview and v3.0 after
software optimizations, including a 17 percent BERT improvement
[@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]. This vendor-reported comparison is an
example of continuing software enablement, not a dependable improvement rate
or a revision of the hardware's design-time result.

## What Carries Forward to the New Study

The transfer test can be applied in five steps.

1. Name the source and target decisions.
2. Separate the source system into transfer units.
3. Identify the dependency that changed for each unit.
4. Assign reuse, refresh, rerun, requalify, recalibrate, adapt, retrain,
   replace or retire, narrow, or reject.
5. Require a target check capable of observing the risk introduced by the
   change, plus an integration check for an unchanged neighbor.

The test succeeds only when no target conclusion advances without an
appropriate target check. Applied to the array study, it produces the action
plan in @tbl-ch9-adaptation-disposition. The plan keeps the source record
intact while refusing to make it carry a different claim.

| **Treatment** | **What happens in the target study** |
| --- | --- |
| **Reuse** | Keep the record schema, provenance structure, raw simulator outputs, four judgments, and candidate identities as historical anchors. |
| **Refresh** | Replace the synthetic slice with a trace-backed workload distribution; pin compiler, runtime, mapping, interface, and target objective versions. |
| **Rerun** | Define the legal target space and evaluation budget, then evaluate the reference and target alternatives under the new workload, mapping, memory path, offload costs, and decision rule. |
| **Requalify** | Compare SCALE-Sim ordering with a sampled property-specific reference in the target region, then state where the unchanged cheap screen remains supported. |
| **Recalibrate** | If the screen retains the required inputs and semantics but its numerical relationship or threshold changed, fit that relationship on a target calibration set and verify it on separate held-out target cases. |
| **Adapt** | Update the represented project state, tool interfaces, environment configuration, routing policy, and verification path for the implementation-facing target. Derive functional references and properties separately where practical. |
| **Retrain** | Retrain only a learned component whose target support is inadequate and for which suitable target data and held-out checks exist. |
| **Replace or retire** | Remove a method, wrapper, environment component, or check that cannot support the target versions or required failure classes. |
| **Narrow** | Treat 32 by 32 only as the retained reference candidate for the new comparison. |
| **Reject** | Do not transfer the source 1 percent score, AI-contribution result, failed mechanism explanation, or pending recommendation into the RTL decision. |

: **The adaptation keeps the record and reopens the claim.** Reuse of an
artifact does not imply reuse of its conclusion. {#tbl-ch9-adaptation-disposition tbl-colwidths="[20,70]"}

Reuse protects the historical artifacts. Refresh and rerun rebuild the target
state and observations. Requalification tests whether an unchanged component
still applies, while recalibration changes a numerical relationship or
threshold. Retrain, replace, and retire apply only to components that need
those actions. Narrow and reject constrain what may be claimed. This plan
authorizes a new study, not the 32 by 32 freeze.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Reuse the record, not the conclusion"}
Do not freeze the 32 by 32 array or its interface from the result in
@sec-running-the-loop.
Use it as the reference candidate in an implementation-readiness study brief
that still must be frozen. The source study remains closed, and the target
decision remains open until the new study plan is fixed and its obligations
are tested.
:::

The study brief now has explicit tests and boundaries
(@tbl-ch9-target-tests).

These rows are not a universal signoff checklist. Each comes from a specific
difference between the closed source study and the target decision. The source
result is preserved, the changed condition creates a new test obligation, and
the plan states what can proceed if that test is absent. A different
target would produce a different set.

| **Target obligation** | **Minimum test** | **Boundary if absent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workload coverage | Trace-backed common and tail cases, versioned with stated exclusions. | No representativeness claim. |
| Candidate comparison | Predeclare the legal target space, search and evaluation budgets, credible comparator, decision rule, and a sensitivity or resolving-power check. | No claim outside evaluated candidates and no comparative AI-contribution claim when the study cannot distinguish its arms. |
| Mapping and software path | Compiler-generated end-to-end execution using pinned mapping, compiler, runtime, driver and firmware versions where applicable, and interface versions. | No claim that the array is usable by the target stack. |
| Interface and memory cost | Offload granularity, bandwidth, traffic, latency, and a calibrated or validated energy-and-power model with execution rate, duty cycle, leakage and idle power, and the complete subsystem boundary. | No 3\ W or system-speedup claim. |
| Cheap-screen validity | Representative random or stratified target samples checked against a separate property-specific reference path, with class-specific error limits, uncertainty, the ability to decline a prediction when support is inadequate, and a later drift audit. | SCALE-Sim remains a source-study tool, not a target decision filter. |
| RTL behavior | Independently derived reference tests and properties where practical, plus lint, functional simulation, synthesis, and formal checks within their stated reach; add fault- and threat-model properties required by the target. | No implementation-readiness, reliability, or security claim beyond the properties checked. |
| Physical behavior | Pin the selected 3\ nm-class low-power process design kit, libraries, and process, voltage, and temperature conditions; then test area and floorplan feasibility, relevant setup and hold corners, congestion and design rules, routed dynamic and leakage power, power delivery, and electrothermal behavior. | No signoff, tapeout, or physical-feasibility claim. |
| Containment | Exercise each proposed bypass, disable, guardband, isolation mechanism, or fallback against the fault or attack it is intended to contain. | No claim that the implementation can contain or recover from that failure. |
| Design-process comparison | Repeat the target study against a credible alternative and record human, machine, tool, and review cost. | No claim that the complete AI-assisted system improves the design process. |

: **Each obligation changes what the next evaluation must measure.** Untested
boundaries remain visible rather than being absorbed into a general claim.
{#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[22,46,32]"}

The first four rows define the target workload, comparison, executable path,
and product-path costs. The next four establish where the cheap screen,
RTL checks, physical checks, and containment mechanisms can support a claim.
The final row passes a complete AI-assisted workflow comparison to
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. It does not perform that evaluation here.

Three compact stress tests show how the same reasoning applies beyond
the array study (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests). Each names the transfer unit,
the dependency that changed, a valid action, and the target check. The examples
are deliberately different. One concerns a learned physical-design predictor,
one concerns continuing software improvement on fixed hardware, and one
concerns a physical defect that software could not correct.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learned placement or congestion predictor trained on one process, library, and design family [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet; @WangEtAl2025ChiPBench] | The target process, library, netlist family, placement flow, or routed-result definition changes. | Requalify the unchanged predictor first; recalibrate, adapt, retrain, or retire it only after identifying what no longer holds. | Measure class-specific target error and decision quality against routed target results kept separate from calibration or training data. |
| H100 software-optimization result reported between MLPerf Training v2.1 preview and v3.0 [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] | A later compiler, library, workload, or hardware generation changes the paired configuration. | Narrow the published improvement to its reported versions and workload; rerun the comparison for the new pair. | Repeat the end-to-end workload measurement with both hardware and software versions pinned and the same result definition. |
| Cougar Point containment and correction result [@Intel2011CougarPoint] | The target defect and the mechanisms able to reach it differ. Intel's announced permanent correction used revised silicon and repair or replacement; the release did not present firmware as the correction. | Do not assume a firmware-only remedy can reach a silicon defect; use a correction or containment mechanism matched to the failure. | Exercise the corrected silicon and any proposed containment against the target failure class before claiming correction. |

: **The same transfer test applies to learned, software, and physical
components.** The action follows the changed dependency, and the target check
must observe the failure or improvement being claimed.
{#tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests tbl-colwidths="[24,29,23,24]"}

The learned-predictor case prevents a familiar model name from substituting for
target support. The H100 case preserves the reported result without turning 17
percent into a general software-improvement rate. The Cougar Point case
preserves the lesson about failure reach without assuming that every silicon
defect requires the same remedy. All three retain useful source knowledge while
refusing to move the conclusion beyond the configuration that produced it.

This plan does not change decision rights. Automated components may propose or
screen candidates inside the declared study.
Rejection, waivers, the architecture freeze, signoff, and tapeout remain with
the named roles defined in @sec-what-architect-owns.

The adaptation decision is complete even though the target architecture
decision is not. The study structure and reference candidate can move forward.
The source conclusion cannot.

## Open Research Questions

Transfer is not a property of a result in isolation. It depends on which data,
models, interfaces, tools, and conclusions remain valid after the target
changes.

**Finding the transfer boundary.** The first problem is to identify what a
change actually invalidates without reopening unrelated work.

**How can a design system trace a target change to exactly the components and
conclusions it affects?** Dependencies cross data, represented state, software,
hardware, tools, and checks, and many of those dependencies are not explicit in
current project artifacts.

**When does an adapted target require a new architecture study rather than a
local refresh or rerun?** Small version changes can alter a decisive interface
or measurement meaning, while large implementation changes may leave a narrow
claim intact.

**Requalifying reused capability.** Reuse is useful only when target evidence
establishes where the reused component still works.

**How can validated coverage be estimated under target drift without sending
every case through the expensive reference path?** Sampling and uncertainty
must expose class-specific failures while the target distribution continues to
change.

**How should hardware and software claims be requalified when their versions
change at different rates?** A fast software result may depend on a hardware
snapshot that is already stale, while a hardware commitment must survive
software behavior that did not exist when it was evaluated.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer components, not conclusions"}
Separate the source system into the parts that might transfer. Every changed
dependency requires a target action and check, and every unchanged part still
requires an integration check when a neighbor changes. Narrow or reject the
source conclusion until the target comparison supports it.
:::

The completed source record remains useful. Its candidate identities, raw
simulator outputs, failed explanation, four judgments, and provenance limits
do not disappear when the target changes. What disappears is the right to read
a synthetic, simulator-local no-change result as an RTL and interface decision
for the spatial-tracking subsystem.

The source-target comparison explains why. Workload, observability, interface
span, reversibility, and consequence changed, so the target requires new
workload, mapping, RTL, physical, thermal, and containment checks. Those
conditions are not a general checklist. They are the material differences in
this design problem.

The component map then assigns work precisely. Historical data can be reused
while target data is refreshed. Project state and interfaces can be adapted. A
predictor or cheap screen can be requalified and, when its numerical
relationship changed without invalidating its inputs or semantics,
recalibrated. A learned component can be retrained when target data and
held-out checks justify it. Unsupported methods, tools, and checks can be
replaced or retired. Architecture and AI-contribution conclusions receive a
different treatment. They are narrowed to the source conditions or rejected
for the target until the comparison is repeated.

Transfer also depends on the complete product path. A local array gain must
repay startup, data movement, compiler, runtime, and maintenance costs before it
supports a system result. A cheap check can remove expensive work only for the
target cases it settles within validated error limits. Hardware and software
results remain tied to the versions, workloads, and measurement conditions that
produced them. A newer result may reopen a dependent claim, but it does not
overwrite the older result.

These principles support a completed adaptation plan and an unresolved
architecture commitment. Keep 32 by 32 as the reference candidate. Refresh the
workload and software state, rerun the target comparison, requalify the cheap
screen and recalibrate it only if warranted, adapt the target environment and
verification path, and add the implementation checks that the source study
never ran. Do not transfer the local score, AI-contribution comparison, failed
mechanism explanation, or pending recommendation.

@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect receives the varied target conditions,
validated cheap-check scope, versioned hardware-software state, implementation
checks, and requirement for comparison with a credible alternative. It
evaluates the complete AI-assisted design system and the cost of obtaining its
results. The architecture commitment remains a separate decision.
